abstract: Chronotypes are circadian variants in timing of a behaviour. In humans, some studies have associated differences in sleep timing and quality with underlying circadian clock driven chronotypes although confounding genetic, environmental and social factors complicate the interpretation of these relationships. Here, we present evidence from artificially selected early and late eclosion chronotype populations of Drosophila melanogaster which suggest that divergence in chronotype can lead to correlated evolution of changes in sleep architecture. We find that early chronotype flies exhibit greater sleep fragmentation and shorter sleep latency during night, whereas late flies showed weaker and less consistent changes in the same direction. These differences were broadly seen for both sexes. We also show that environmental cues like temperature cycles can modulate sleep timing and enhance chronotype differences, while increasing light intensity delayed nighttime sleep timing similarly across chronotypes. Additionally, when sleep was disrupted by mechanical perturbations, late flies could not recover lost sleep to the same degree as early and control in a time-of-day dependent manner. In contrast, following simulated jetlag-induced circadian misalignment, early flies showed a greater increase in daytime sleep after phase advances. Our findings suggest that sleep and circadian traits can coevolve, offering insights into the complex interactions between chronotypes and sleep architecture. These populations provide an evolutionary model to investigate how circadian timing, sleep architecture and homeostatic regulation may be linked.
